item.title: A Recursive Module-Coupling Algorithm for Computing Low-Energy Eigenstates
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Recursive module-coupling constructs low-energy subspaces directly from products of module eigenstates on an equal footing without iterative sweeps. Yields variational ground and excited states with computational speedup over DMRG in the moderate-accuracy regime.

Grade 0.374 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “A variational eigenvalue solver on a photonic quantum processor” · Dihang Sun, Nannan Ma, Ching Hua Lee, Tianqi Chen, Jiangbin Gong

Figure

Cumulative CPU time versus system size for the modular projected eigensolver compared to DMRG across target error densities. Panel (a) shows ground-state energy convergence, while panel (b) shows simultaneous convergence for the four lowest eigenstates.

Asks

How can low-energy many-body eigenstates be efficiently computed and hierarchically prepared on gate-based quantum hardware without full-space variational sweeps?

Before

DMRG optimizes global matrix product states through sequential sweeps to obtain excited states one by one.

But

Accuracy degrades under strong inter-module coupling and hardware noise. Tested on 1D transverse-field Ising chains up to L=80 classically and L=30 on IBM quantum hardware.

Tools

recursive block renormalization · block encoders · variational quantum eigensolvers · IBM Quantum processors · Qiskit

Abstract

Finding the eigenstates of a many-body Hamiltonian is a fundamental challenge in physics and computational science. Since the search space grows exponentially with system size, numerous classical and quantum algorithms have been developed to address this problem. A practical strategy is to identify a physics-informed low-dimensional subspace that effectively accommodates the low-lying eigenstates, thereby reducing the computational complexity. In this paper, we propose a recursive module-coupling algorithm, which iteratively treats a system as a composition of locally-coupled smaller modules, with low-energy subspace estimated successively according to the same recursive structure. Unlike the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) approach that optimizes a global matrix product state through repeated local sweeps and obtains excited states sequentially, our algorithm constructs a physically tailored variational basis from module eigenstates and obtains several low-energy states on an equal footing, leading to substantial speedups if targeting moderate accuracy. Our proposed method further leads naturally to a recursive quantum variational algorithm, providing a systematic and modular circuit-construction framework compatible with contemporary gate-based quantum architectures. At each recursive level, block encoders are trained to map logical basis states onto the retained physical subspace, within which a variational circuit is subsequently optimized.Such a quantum-circuit implementation provides not only a quantum multistate eigensolver, but also a systematic prescription for hierarchically constructing quantum state-preparation circuits. Classical simulations demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method, whereas experiments on IBM quantum processors show that eigenstate preparation with reasonable fidelities is achievable even in the current NISQ era.

item.title: Quantum Representation Learning Beyond Pairwise Fidelity
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Transition-probability interfaces possess continuous blind directions. Adding normalized coherent moment q~− from two-copy interference captures 4-state Bargmann invariants and cuts mean out-of-distribution phase error by 86% at fixed shot budget Ntot=393216.

Grade 0.369 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Machine Learning in Feature Hilbert Spaces” · Junpeng Hou, Changbin Lu

Figure

Quantum circuit sequence for measuring the multistate relational observables: loading pair superpositions into address registers, selecting overlap amplitudes into a target branch to measure p−, and measuring two copies with an address SWAP to evaluate second moment q−=Tr⁡Σ−2.

Asks

What information is lost when a quantum representation learner only receives pairwise transition probabilities, and can missing multistate relational invariants be measured and trained directly?

But

Simulated four-photon benchmark with independent preparation drift; advantage over fidelity baseline relies on fixed two-probe measurement setup unless mode-engineering protects orthogonality (x23=0).

Tools

Two-copy destructive SWAP interferometry · Parameter-shift rule variational optimization · Address-controlled overlap state loader · Canonical correlation analysis (CCA)

Abstract

Quantum contrastive, metric, and self-supervised learning often expose encoded quantum states to the learner through transition probabilities, especially fidelity. Quantum states are known to possess higher-order relational invariants, but their consequences for learned representations remain unclear. Here we show that a transition-probability-only learning interface can possess exact continuous blind directions in certain quantum-state families. We recover this missing information with a batch operator, built from coherent overlap amplitudes and negative masking, where its second moment q₋ retains four-state interference. Moreover, q₋ is directly measurable through two-copy interference and can enter variational learning via methods like parameter shift. In relational quartets derived from toric-code and double-semion states, this fidelity-blind signal encodes inequivalent modular data despite identical pairwise fidelities. Finally, in a four-photon benchmark with preparation drift, augmenting all six pairwise fidelities at two orthogonal probes with the corresponding normalized q₋ reduces the mean out-of-distribution phase error by 86% at equal total shot budget. These results establish multistate relational observables as measurable, trainable, and physically consequential signals for quantum representation learning beyond pairwise fidelity.

item.title: Variational preparation of thermofield double states for SYK models via multi-angle QAOA: sequential angle pruning for circuit reduction
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Top-down sequential angle pruning (SAP and objective-aware OSAP) removes 88.8%--92.1% of nonlocal Pauli-string evolutions in multi-angle QAOA while maintaining approximately 95% average fidelity for binary sparse N=10 SYK thermofield double states at β=10.

Grade 0.366 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “A variational eigenvalue solver on a photonic quantum processor” · Haji Muhammad Husnain Ashfaq, Moongul Byun, Keun-Young Kim

Figure

Target thermofield double state infidelity 𝔼J[1−F] plotted against the retained block count 𝒮 for the binary sparse N=10 SYK model across β=0.1,1,10. It shows SAP and OSAP maintaining low infidelity down to small block counts compared to batch-pruning baselines.

Asks

How can gate counts and circuit depth in multi-angle QAOA be systematically reduced while preserving high fidelity for thermofield double state preparation?

But

Evaluated in classical numerical simulations for N=8 and N=10 Majorana fermions over 20 disorder realizations; no quantum hardware noise or measurement shot noise modeled.

Tools

multi-angle QAOA (ma-QAOA) · sequential angle pruning (SAP) · objective-aware SAP (OSAP) · Jordan-Wigner transformation · sparse and dense SYK models

Abstract

Variational preparation of thermofield double (TFD) states can require deep quantum circuits, particularly for interacting many-body systems. Reducing these circuits while retaining high fidelity is therefore crucial for TFD-state preparation on noisy quantum processors. We study this problem by applying the multi-angle quantum approximate optimization algorithm (ma-QAOA) to TFD-state preparation and introducing two top-down sequential angle-pruning algorithms. Starting from the optimized initial ma-QAOA circuit, both algorithms sequentially remove Pauli-string evolutions with small optimized angles and reoptimize the remaining parameters after each removal. We apply these algorithms to Gaussian and binary Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev (SYK) models in both dense and sparse cases. We find that ma-QAOA prepares the target TFD states with high fidelity and that sequential small-angle pruning retains high fidelity while reducing the circuit depth, particularly at low temperature. Moreover, using the post-reoptimization cost in sequential small-angle pruning further improves the fidelity. For the binary sparse N=10 SYK model at β=10, 88.8%--92.1% of the nonlocal Pauli-string evolutions are removed while retaining an average fidelity of approximately 95%. Finally, we propose extensions of the sequential pruning algorithms toward quantum--classical hybrid implementation.

item.title: Purification of photonic graph states
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Photonic CSS, GHZ, and arbitrary stabilizer graph states are purified using only linear optics and photon detectors via transversal type-I fusions, reaching per-round success probability up to 1/2. For 3-qubit (4-qubit) GHZ states under depolarization error pdep=0.05, two cascaded rounds raise fidelity from F≈0.86 (F≈0.81) to F=0.988 (F=0.981).

Grade 0.355 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Power of data in quantum machine learning” · Matthias C. Löbl, Aliki A. Capatos, Ming Lai Chan, Peter Lodahl, Anders Søndberg Sørensen, Stefano Paesani

Figure

GHZ state fidelity plotted against qubit count (n=2 to 8) for depolarization noise pdep=0.05 across zero, one (bit- or phase-flip), and two cascaded purification rounds.

Asks

How can noisy photonic graph states generated by quantum emitters be purified without deterministic entangling gates?

Before

was 192 photons on average to produce a 3-qubit GHZ state probabilistically with all-linear optics; emitter-based generation with time-multiplexed two-round purification requires 96 photons.

But

Assumes error-free linear-optics circuits. First-order photon loss doubles for small loss rates pl under phase-flip purification.

Tools

transversal type-I fusion · polarizing beam splitters and photon-number-resolving detectors · quantum emitters in waveguides · stabilizer and CSS formalism

Abstract

Graph states constitute the main building block for quantum computing with photons. Quantum emitters with a hosted spin can deterministically generate photonic graph states, strongly lowering the overhead of multiplexing highly probabilistic linear-optics graph state generation. However, they generally suffer from various noise sources, resulting in reduced fidelities of the produced states. To mitigate this issue, we develop purification schemes for entangled photonic states. We first develop purification schemes to purify arbitrary photonic GHZ and other CSS states, which we generalize to all photonic graph states and stabilizer states. The proposed purification schemes have a high success probability of up to 1/2 and require only linear optics and photon detectors. We optimize cascaded purification schemes for various graph states, taking into account phenomenological Pauli errors or physical noise in time-bin-encoded graph state generation with quantum emitters.

item.title: A quantum oracle separation between QMA(2) and QMA
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Constructed unitary oracle U separating the classes: 𝖰𝖬𝖠U≠𝖰𝖬𝖠(2)U. For any ε+δ<1, any (ε,δ)-disentangler requires input size exponential in output qubits, resolving Watrous's no-disentanglers conjecture.

Grade 0.351 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum machine learning models built from interference and oracle algorithms,…” · John Bostanci, Sabee Grewal, Jonas Haferkamp, Andrew Huang, Yeongwoo Hwang, Anand Natarajan, Chinmay Nirkhe

Figure

Plot of polynomial p(x) versus index x∈{0,…,N}, showing p(0)=0 and p(j)≈1 for j≥1, illustrating the approximate degree lower bound reduction to the OR function.

Asks

Can a 𝖰𝖬𝖠(2) verifier solve a quantum oracle problem efficiently that no 𝖰𝖬𝖠 verifier can?

Before

Unconditional lower bounds held only for (0,0)-disentanglers (Aaronson et al. 2009), quasipolynomial bounds for exponentially small ε+δ (Harrow, Natarajan, and Wu 2019), or strong disentanglers (Akibue, Kato, and Tani 2025).

But

Unitary quantum oracle setting (classical oracle separation remains open); asymptotic lower bounds.

Tools

unitarily invariant polynomial method · symmetric and antisymmetric subspace projectors · approximate degree reduction to OR · in-place witness guessing amplification

Abstract

We find a quantum oracle relative to which QMA ≠QMA(2). As a consequence, we resolve the no-disentanglers conjecture of Watrous: for every ε+δ<1, any (ε,δ)-disentangler requires input size exponential in the number of output qubits. Our proof combines the unitarily invariant polynomial method of She and Yuen (ITCS '23) with a new construction based on the symmetric and antisymmetric subspace projectors, reducing the QMA lower bound to the approximate degree of OR.

item.title: Optimal Fusion Strategies for Quantum Computation
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Optimal non-adaptive fusion strategy for a single-qubit stabilizer code is given by its largest non-trivial logical operator containing no non-identity stabilizer substring. A perfect fusion strategy exists whenever this operator has full weight, tolerating failure of all but one physical fusion.

Grade 0.349 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum machine learning models built from interference and oracle algorithms,…” · Kenneth Goodenough, Andrew Landahl, Joon Lee, Antonio Russo, Kevin Thompson

Figure

Schematic of single-qubit logical teleportation via physical pairwise fusions between code blocks L and LA, where failed fusions measure single-qubit Pauli observables and successful fusions perform Bell-state measurements.

Asks

Which quantum error-correcting codes and non-adaptive measurement bases admit perfect fusion strategies where only a single physical fusion must succeed?

But

Encodes a single qubit (k=1), non-adaptive strategies only, Pauli basis measurements (X, Y, or Z), noiseless/lossless channels with fusion failure as the sole error source.

Tools

stabilizer formalism · graph codes · local complementation · Paley-Zygmund inequality · random graph theory

Abstract

Logical fusions are important for a number of tasks in quantum information, such as quantum error correction and quantum repeaters. In the photonic setting one must contend with the fact that physical fusions are probabilistic (i.e.~the associated qubits are measured in product bases), which---depending on the failures and the associated bases---can lead to a failure on the logical level. The choice of failure basis of each qubit is known as a fusion strategy, and finding good fusion strategies is important for optimizing performance of fusion-based quantum computation. Here we provide a complete characterization when k=1 qubits are encoded, and in particular characterize those codes and fusion strategies such that all but one physical fusion can fail, i.e.~emphperfect fusion strategies. In doing so, we recover previously known perfect fusion strategies, and find perfect fusion strategies for quantum parity-check codes, answering an open question. We furthermore show that perfect fusion strategies are generic: random $[[n, 1, d]]$ graph codes admit a perfect fusion strategy with probability exponentially close to 1. Additionally we motivate the study of a new graph parameter, namely the maximum degree of a graph at a given vertex taken over all LC-equivalent graphs, by giving a new operationally meaningful interpretation of it.

In the photonic setting one must contend with the fact that physical fusions are probabilistic (i.e.~the associated qubits are measured in product bases), which---depending on the failures and the associated bases---can lead to a failure on the logical level. The choice of failure basis of each qubit is known as a fusion strategy, and finding good fusion strategies is important for optimizing performance of fusion-based quantum computation. Here we provide a complete characterization when k=1 qubits are encoded, and in particular characterize those codes and fusion strategies such that all but one physical fusion can fail, i.e.~emphperfect fusion strategies. In doing so, we recover previously known perfect fusion strategies, and find perfect fusion strategies for quantum parity-check codes, answering an open question. We furthermore show that perfect fusion strategies are generic: random $[[n, 1, d]]$ graph codes admit a perfect fusion strategy with probability exponentially close to 1. Additionally we motivate the study of a new graph parameter, namely the maximum degree of a graph at a given vertex taken over all LC-equivalent graphs, by giving a new operationally meaningful interpretation of it.

item.title: Quantum Meta-Complexity Is All You Need: Characterizing One-Way Puzzles via Time-Bounded Kolmogorov Complexity
item.description:
Worth a look new result — One-way puzzles exist if and only if 𝖦𝖺𝗉-pK𝗊t∗ is weakly quantum-average-hard over quantumly samplable distributions at subexponential time bound t∗(n)=2n/2poly(n). Any string sampled by a QPT machine with probability δ admits a description length log⁡(1/δ)+O(log⁡(nT)) decodable in time O(1/δ⋅(nT)O(1)).

Grade 0.343 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Power of data in quantum machine learning” · Morteza Saberikamarposhti

Figure

Dependency graph showing the reduction cycle between one-way puzzles, exponentially-far non-uniform quantum PRGs, 𝖦𝖺𝗉-pK𝗊t hardness, and quantum probability estimation. Blue edges highlight where the subexponential or conjectured polynomial quantum coding theorems close the equivalence.

Asks

Can one-way puzzles be characterized by the average-case hardness of a computable, time-bounded quantum Kolmogorov complexity measure rather than uncomputable plain Kolmogorov complexity?

Before

One-way puzzles were characterized by the average-case hardness of plain, uncomputable Kolmogorov complexity K (t=∞) over quantumly samplable distributions (Hiroka and Morimae; Cavalar et al.).

But

Adversaries are restricted to uniform QPT; characterization at polynomial time bounds poly(n) remains conditional on a conjectured polynomial-time quantum coding theorem.

Tools

probabilistic time-bounded quantum program complexity pK_q^t · quantum rejection sampling · amplitude amplification · almost-universal hashing · quantum probability estimation via bitwise extrapolation

Abstract

We initiate the time-bounded meta-complexity program for quantum cryptography. Recent work characterizes one-way puzzles, the minimal search primitive of quantum cryptography without one-way functions, by the average-case hardness of approximating the plain, uncomputable Kolmogorov complexity over quantumly samplable distributions; the classical program of Liu and Pass, by contrast, lives at polynomial time bounds. We define a probabilistic time-bounded quantum program complexity pKq^t for classical strings and prove two unconditional theorems. First, a quantum coding theorem: any string output by a quantum polynomial-time sampler with probability delta admits a description of the information-theoretically optimal length log(1/delta) plus logarithmic terms, decodable by a quantum machine in time O(sqrt(1/delta)) times a polynomial, via amplitude amplification over the coherently executed sampler. Second, an exact characterization at subexponential time: one-way puzzles exist if and only if the gap problem for pKq at time bound 2^(n/2) poly(n) is weakly quantum-average-hard, refining the plain-complexity characterizations. We then isolate the polynomial-time coding theorem as the single load-bearing open conjecture of the program, prove that it implies the full polynomial-time characterization, analyze why the classical derandomization proof resists quantization, and formulate a relativized barrier conjecture delimiting string-valued meta-complexity at one-way puzzles. Conjectures are labeled as such throughout.
